metadata.title: Local Ranking Problem on the BrowseGraph

extraction_notes.note: The paper's findings are empirical observations read off tables and figures; the key ones are emitted as claim nodes with rigor numerical, while the tables and figures themselves (only in floats/images) are not nodes.

pseudocode_steps mis-parsed algorithm2e's two-body \eIf: it truncated the \For/\eIf step statements (ASP5, ASP7, ASP9) after the then-branch and parented the else-branch lines to ASP7. Overriding 'keep as returned', the three statements were re-sliced verbatim to their matching closing braces and the else-branch lines reparented to ASP9.
Dropped the comment-only pseudocode line (/* For each step ... */) and the trailing caption fragment after \Return as non-operations; steps renumbered.
LRP is stated both in the Introduction and in Related Work (Chen et al.); the Introduction's two-sentence formulation was kept as the single node.
theorem or remark: Bressan and Pretto's impossibility result is only summarized in words, but it is a cited result stated in full, so it is an external theorem.

nodes.statement: The Local Ranking Problem (LRP) was first introduced by Chen et al. in 2004, who addressed the problem to approximate/update the PageRank of individual nodes, without performing a large-scale computation on the entire graph.
conclusions: The Local Ranking Problem (LRP) was first introduced by Chen et al.
in 2004, who addressed the problem to approximate/update the PageRank of individual nodes, without performing a large-scale computation on the entire graph.
nodes.raw_latex: The \textit{Local Ranking Problem} (LRP) was first introduced by Chen \emph{et al.}~\cite{Chen2004} in $2004$, who addressed the problem to approximate/update the PageRank of individual nodes, without performing a large-scale computation on the entire graph.
nodes.clean_text: The Local Ranking Problem (LRP) was first introduced by Chen et al. in 2004, who addressed the problem to approximate/update the PageRank of individual nodes, without performing a large-scale computation on the entire graph.

nodes.statement: In 2008 the problem was reconsidered by Bar-Yossef and Mashiach, where they simplified the problem calculating a local Reverse PageRank proving that it is more feasible and computationally cheaper, as the reverse natural graphs tend to have low in-degree maintaining a fast PageRank convergence.
conclusions: In 2008 the problem was reconsidered by Bar-Yossef and Mashiach, where they simplified the problem calculating a local Reverse PageRank proving that it is more feasible and computationally cheaper, as the reverse natural graphs tend to have low in-degree maintaining a fast PageRank convergence.
nodes.raw_latex: In $2008$ the problem was reconsidered by Bar-Yossef and Mashiach~\cite{Bar-Yossef2008}, where they simplified the problem calculating a local {\it Reverse PageRank} proving that it is more feasible and computationally cheaper, as the reverse natural graphs tend to have low in-degree maintaining a fast PageRank convergence.
nodes.clean_text: In 2008 the problem was reconsidered by Bar-Yossef and Mashiach, where they simplified the problem calculating a local Reverse PageRank proving that it is more feasible and computationally cheaper, as the reverse natural graphs tend to have low in-degree maintaining a fast PageRank convergence.

nodes.statement: Bressan and Pretto proved that, in the general case, an efficient local ranking algorithm does not exist, and in order to compute a correct ranking it is necessary to visit at least a number of nodes linear in the size of the input graph.
conclusions: Bressan and Pretto proved that, in the general case, an efficient local ranking algorithm does not exist, and in order to compute a correct ranking it is necessary to visit at least a number of nodes linear in the size of the input graph.
nodes.raw_latex: Bressan and Pretto~\cite{Bressan2011} proved that, in the general case, an efficient local ranking algorithm does not exist, and in order to compute a {\it correct} ranking it is necessary to visit at least a number of nodes linear in the size of the input graph.
nodes.clean_text: Bressan and Pretto proved that, in the general case, an efficient local ranking algorithm does not exist, and in order to compute a correct ranking it is necessary to visit at least a number of nodes linear in the size of the input graph.

nodes.statement: A similar problem was studied by Andersen et al., where their goal was to compute the PageRank contributions in a local graph motivated by the problem of detecting link-spam: given a page, its PageRank contributors are the pages that contribute most to its rank; contributors are used for spam detection since you can quickly identify the set of pages that contribute significantly to the PageRank of a suspicious page.

nodes.statement: logPr leftarrow initialize ~vector ~with ~size ~G_k.length()\; n leftarrow total number of nodes\; x_j leftarrow choose (random) starting node in G_k\; BlankLine /* For each step, compute a random walk in G_k, and compare the probability to be in all the other G */\\ For s leftarrow 1 TO steps BlankLine /* Pick the next node of G_k with random walk */\\ x_k = next\_node( G_k, x_j )\; BlankLine For ileftarrow 0 KwTo G.length() leftlangle k_outrightrangle leftarrow get\_outdegree(n_p)\; eIf leftlangle k_outrightrangle == 0 logPr[ i ] leftarrow logPr[ i ] + log( 1 / n )\; p_i(x) = (1-alpha) / n\; Pd_x_j leftarrow get\_prob\_distribution(G_i,~x_j)\; S_x_j leftarrow get\_successors(G_i,~x_j)\; If x_k in S_x_j p_i(x) leftarrow p_i(x) + alpha * Pd_x_j(x_k)\; logPr[ i ] leftarrow logPr[ i ] + log( p_i(x) )\; Return~logPr captionRandomSurfer(k,~alpha,~steps,~G)

nodes.statement: For each subgraph G_i, we simulated a random surfer moving around in G_i (i.e., calling the function RandomSurfer(i, alpha, steps, G)), computing at each step (i.e., page visited) the probability of the surfer to navigate in each subgraph G_1, dots G_7: we expect that the probability corresponding to G_i will increase at each step, and will eventually dominate all the others.
nodes.raw_latex:
For each subgraph $G_i$, we simulated a random
surfer moving around in $G_i$ (\emph{i.e.}, calling the function \texttt{RandomSurfer}(i, $\alpha$, steps, G)), computing at each step (\emph{i.e.}, page visited) the probability of the surfer to navigate in each subgraph $G_1$, \dots $G_7$: 
we expect that the probability corresponding to $G_i$ will increase at each step, and will 
eventually dominate all the others.
